summary:
Astrocare is an offline, on-board health companion for astronauts on long missions such as Mars. It is a web prototype that combines a daily readiness score, vitals, sleep, hydration and cabin CO₂ monitoring, a digital twin that previews bone and muscle loss, mood check-ins, an offline medic guide, radiation tracking and crew bonding tools. An “Earth Window” shows a loved one’s message over NASA satellite imagery when a check-in looks heavy.

It is built around NASA’s Human Research Program five hazards of spaceflight. Solar Shield uses NASA DONKI space-weather data for radiation alerts, and the Earth Window uses NASA Black Marble and NASA POWER data. Colour-coded indicators and simple explanations help astronauts assess their health and act on it themselves.

With a 3 to 22 minute communication delay each way on Mars, astronauts cannot rely on Earth for real-time help. Astrocare catches small problems early and protects mental health as well as physical health, with privacy-first sharing. It supports flight surgeons and never replaces them. The crew data is simulated.
details:
What it does: Astrocare is an on-board health and wellbeing companion for astronauts on long missions, such as a trip to Mars. It gathers health indicators, shows their status at a glance, and guides the astronaut on what to do next. It answers NASA’s five hazards of spaceflight: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields and hostile closed environments.

How it works:

  • The astronaut logs the six indicators named in the challenge: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood. Hydration, exercise, reaction time and cabin air add to them.
  • A colour-coded Capability Scan combines 15 factors into physical, cognitive, psychological and recovery scores. Each score is capped by its weakest factor, so one red flag can’t be averaged away.
  • The Digital Twin shows where bone and muscle could be by day 180 if the astronaut changes sleep or exercise.
  • Solar Shield tracks a radiation dose budget and uses real solar-flare data from NASA DONKI.
  • Offline Medic gives step-by-step guidance with no connection, which matters with a 3 to 22 minute delay to Earth.
  • Calm Orbit, the Constellation of Loved Ones and the Earth Window protect mental health.
  • Fly Home zooms from space to the astronaut’s hometown in Esri World Imagery. It adds nearby attractions from the Africa GeoPortal, and weather for that place from NASA POWER.
  • Zib the pet, daily streaks and a social-style feed keep healthy habits going.
  • All logic runs in the browser, so it works offline. The prototype uses simulated crew and vitals.

Benefits:

  • Astronauts can assess themselves without waiting for Earth.
  • Warnings are never hidden by averaging.
  • Care covers body, mind and connection to home.
  • The same offline design could serve remote clinics, polar bases and other places where help is far away.

Intended impact: Earlier detection of health problems, and a calmer, better-connected crew on missions where help is minutes or hours away. It also shows how space health tools can support remote communities on Earth, including in Africa.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, hosted on Vercel. NASA POWER, NASA DONKI and NASA GIBS. Esri World Imagery, the Africa GeoPortal and OpenStreetMap. Google Fonts.

Creativity: One app joins medicine and emotion: a gamified pet and streak (Zib), a personalised feed, and a flight home over real satellite imagery. A weakest-factor safeguard keeps the scores honest.

Factors we considered:

  • Realism: vitals are simulated and thresholds are illustrative, not clinical. It is not a medical device and not endorsed by NASA.
  • Privacy: crew sharing is consent-based.
  • Accessibility: reduced-motion support.
  • Connectivity: it works offline.
